newsitem.title: USA: Dow Jones down on IBM; Nasdaq hits new high.
newsitem.headline: Dow Jones down on IBM; Nasdaq hits new high.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell Wednesday after Wall Street was turned off by International Business Machines Corp.'s earnings, but the Nasdaq Composite index powered to another record high on upbeat results from other technology companies.

The 30-stock Dow Jones industrial average ended down 33.87 points at 6,850.03, and virtually all of the loss stemmed from IBM, which tumbled 10-3/8 to 157-5/8. The drop in the index snapped a four-session string of record closes.
The Nasdaq gained 11.09 points to 1,388.06, beating Tuesday's record close of 1,376.97. The Standard & Poor's 500 rose and NYSE Composite indexes also set new highs.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,301 to 1,186 on heavy volume of 585 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Beyond the drop in IBM, the overall market's performance was mixed.

But the spotlight was fixed squarely on Big Blue, the computer giant whose results prompted many Wall Street analysts to trim their earnings estimates, indicating earlier expectations for the company had run ahead of reality.
"Rather than easily achieve Street estimates, IBM appeared to be huffing and puffing," said Steve Milunovich, an analyst at Morgan Stanley.

Elsewhere, high technology and other big-name stocks extended their rally as earnings news remained broadly positive. According to data provided by I/B/E/S Inc., 56 percent of companies that have reported earnings so far have beaten estimates, with 27 percent falling short.

But some analysts voiced concern about the IBM sell-off, not only because of what it suggested about the outlook for corporate profits but because of what it said about the current psychology of the market.
"You almost get the sense that if a company reports in line (with estimates), the stock's going down," said Melissa Brown, director of quantitative research at Prudential Securities.
"We're going on three years of fairly continuous positive surprises and companies aren't going to be able to keep that up forever," she said.

Another concern was that the increasingly strong dollar eroded IBM's revenue growth in the quarter, an issue that extends well beyond the technology sphere to all multinational companies based in the United States.

"Is this an isolated occurrence? I don't think so," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co. "This foreshadows the real problem of 1997 because one of the pillars of this market has been earnings growth."

The strong dollar hurts U.S. companies doing business in other countries, Metz said, because it reduces the value of international sales and inhibits the companies' ability to price products and services competitively in other markets.
In New York trading, the dollar reached a 46-month high against the Japanese yen and a 31-month peak against the German mark. It rose to 119.03 yen and 1.6420 marks.
For all the concern, investors stayed loyal to companies able to generate a pleasant surprise.
Compaq Computer Corp. surged 5-1/8 to 83-3/8 after its fourth quarter earnings beat analysts' estimates.
Norand Corp. soared 13-5/8 to 33 after the maker of mobile data collection and processing systems agreed to be bought by Western Atlas Inc. for $33.50 per share in cash.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 3.51 points to 786.23, a new high. The American Stock Exchange index edged up 0.93 to 590.87.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 1.23 to 412.80, a new high. The average share was up 13 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was at a new high of 7,594.847 up 27.219 or 0.36 percent.
